newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi signals rates must fall further.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi signals rates must fall further.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Thursday that Italian interest rates had not fallen as much as he had wanted during his first year in office. The rates came down by three percentage points.
He made the statement in a speech to a meeting of cooperative societies, a day after talks at the Bank of Italy with governor Antonio Fazio.
No details have emerged from Wednesday's talks.
"Interest rates have fallen by three points since this government has been here," Prodi said in his speech. "It is not as much as I wanted but three points is not to be sniffed at."
He said each percentage point fall saved industry seven trillion lire ($4.2 billion).
Prodi, a former economics professor, told the meeting of the association Confcooperative that the worst of Italy's economic slowdown was behind it.
"If I were still a professor I would say that the recovery has begun. But as prime minister I have to be more prudent. I believe the worst period has past," he said.

Financial market expectations of further cut in the Bank of Italy's key discount rate have risen since inflation figures for April showed a year-on-year rate for the consumer price index of 1.7 percent, down from 2.2 percent in March.
Fazio has used declining inflation in the past to cut rate, lowering the discount rate to 6.75 percent from 7.50 percent the last time he acted on January 21.
This time, however, many analysts believe Fazio is awaiting details of the government's three-year economic programme, due out later this month, and the outcome of French elections.

A fall in official rates triggers lower bank rates, thus helping industry, and allows the government to reduce the costs of servicing Italy's huge public debt, improving its chances of cutting the public deficit.
